for marginalized or disadvantaged groups-such as individuals with lower levels of education-they risk exacerbating existing social inequalities. However, to our knowledge, no studies have yet investigated whether such factors moderate the effectiveness of personality change interventions. Second, baseline levels of personality traits may influence how participants engage with the intervention. For instance, conscientious individuals are more organized and dutiful, which can support adherence and consistent practice (Högdahl et al., 2016). To the extent that greater engagement leads to stronger change during the intervention (Hudson et al., 2019; Olaru et al., 2025), baseline personality may be prognostic of individuals' improvement. Third, prior clinical work has shown that baseline well-being can affect treatment effects. For instance, in meta-analyses, participants with greater symptom severity (i.e., lower well-being) before the start of the study benefited more from interventions relative to control conditions (e.g., Scholten et al., 2023). Fourth, self-regulatory models of personality development suggest that participants' motivation for change as well as the considered feasibility of these changes should affect how much participants change their personality during an intervention (Hennecke et al., 2014). Lastly, as self-reflective processes and behavioral activities represent key intervention pathways that enhance understanding of personal challenges and facilitate active problem solving (e.g., Allemand & Flückiger, 2017), participants' preferences for self-reflective versus behavioral engagement may shape how they respond to the intervention. For personality traits, motivational factors, and engagement preferences, these arguments thus primarily suggest prognostic associations. Whether these characteristics are also prescriptive, that is, predict treatment effects, depends on whether they facilitate change without the intervention as well (see Figure 1).

The Present Research

In the present study, we examine the degree to which the effects of personality change interventions on life and domain satisfaction differ between individuals. We use longitudinal data from the 10-week personality change intervention PEACH (Stieger et al., 2018 (Stieger et al., , 2021) ) to estimate average and individual treatment effects of the intervention (vs. waitlist control) on life satisfaction, average domain satisfaction, and satisfaction with individual domains using the EffectLiteR approach, a multi-group structural equation modeling framework for causal inference (Mayer et al., 2016 (Mayer et al., , 2020)). We test, quantify, and visualize the degree of interindividual differences in treatment effects and, crucially, predict treatment effects from baseline variables assessed at pretest, consistent with a prescriptive approach. For baseline variables, we focus on demographic characteristics (age, gender, relationship status, education level), baseline personality traits (Big Five self-and observer-reports), baseline well-being (satisfaction, self-esteem), motivational factors (change goal strength, change goal commitment and attainability, belief about the changeability of personality), and engagement preferences (preference for self-reflective and behavioral engagement).

Method Participants

This study presents a secondary analysis of data from participants of the PEACH study (Stieger et al., 2018). The analyses were based on the Starters sample, which included 875 individuals actually starting the intervention (for a CONSORT diagram, see Supplemental Figure S1; Stieger et al., 2021). This sample size was determined by an a priori power analysis for the primary study outcomes (Stieger et al., 2018). Two individuals did not complete the baseline questionnaires or completed them only partially, resulting in a final sample of 873 individuals. These individuals were 54% women, on average 25.6 years old (SDage = 7.2, range = 18-66), 57% were in a relationship, and 40% had a university degree as their highest level of education. As part of the PEACH study, participants were randomly assigned to the PEACH intervention group (n = 655) or a waitlist control group (n = 218).

Participants selected the following change goals: decrease in Neuroticism (n = 256), increase in Extraversion (n = 196), decrease in Extraversion (n = 1), increase in Conscientiousness (n = 226), decrease in Conscientiousness (n = 24), increase in Agreeableness (n = 35), decrease in Agreeableness (n = 57), increase in Openness (n = 63), and decrease in Openness (n = 15).

Of the 873 individuals who started the study, 531 (61%) also completed the posttest, whereas 342 (39%) did not (Supplemental Figure S1). Previous attrition analyses showed that dropout was only weakly related to observed baseline traits (Stieger et al., 2021).

Participants were eligible if they (a) were at least 18 years old, (b) could read German, (c) were not receiving psychotherapeutic or psychiatric treatment, (d) owned a smartphone (Android or iOS) with mobile internet access, and (e) were interested and motivated to participate in an intervention to change a personality trait. Moreover, participants with mental health disorders and other psychosocial problems were excluded. Participants were recruited through university mailings, social media advertisements, flyers, and word-of-mouth. All participants who completed the pretest and follow-up assessment were reimbursed with 25 Swiss Francs. In addition, they could enter a raffle, where winning chances increased with greater participation.

Measures

The following is a brief overview of the measures used in this project. The measures and data collection are described in more detail in Stieger et al. (2018).

Baseline Measures From Pretest

In total, we assessed 34 baseline variables as potential predictors of treatment effect heterogeneity. To assess demographic characteristics, participants were asked about their age, gender (coded as0 = male,1 = female), education level (coded as0 = not university,1 = university), and relationship status (coded as0 = not in a relationship,1 = in a relationship).

Self-ratings of the Big Five personality traits and 15 corresponding facets (i.e., three per domain) were measured with the German version of the 60-item Big Five Inventory-2 (BFI-2; Danner et al., 2016; Soto & John, 2017a), with four items per facet (two reverse-coded) on a 5-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree to5 = strongly agree). Observer ratings were obtained with the German observer-report version of the 30-item BFI-2-S (short version of the BFI-2; Rammstedt et al., 2020; Soto & John, 2017b), covering the same five personality traits with six items each (three reverse-coded) on the same response scale. Participants were asked to forward a weblink to the questionnaire to friends, family members, or their intimate partner, with no limit on the number of recipients. Because not all participants forwarded the weblink and not all recipients responded, the number of observer ratings per participant ranged from zero to seven (M = 1.09, SD = 1.19; at least one rating for 413 participants, 47%). For each participant, we combined all available reports from different observers by computing the average of responses for each item. Self-esteem was assessed using the 10item Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale (RSES; Rosenberg, 1965; five reverse-coded items;1 = strongly disagree to5 = strongly agree). Change goal strength was measured with a single item (Stieger et al., 2018) asking how much participants wanted to change in their selected personality profile (0 = not at all to7 = totally). Change goal commitment and attainability were assessed with an adaptation of the six-item scale developed by Brunstein (1999), with three items each (1 = strongly disagree to5 = strongly agree).

The belief about the changeability of personality was measured with the eight-item implicit theory of personality scale (Dweck, 2013; four reverse-coded items;1 = not true at all to5 = very true). The preferences for self-reflective and behavioral engagement were assessed with six items that were created for the PEACH study, three of which relate to cognitive and three to behavioral activities (1 = strongly disagree to5 = strongly agree).

Outcome Measures From Pretest and Posttest

Life satisfaction was measured using the German version of the five-item Satisfaction With Life Scale (SWLS; Diener et al., 1985; Glaesmer et al., 2011;1 = strongly disagree to5 = strongly agree). In addition, participants were asked to rate their satisfaction with nine specific life domains, each assessed with a single item ( Hudson & Roberts, 2014

Procedure

All procedures of this study were approved by the Ethics Committee of the Philosophical Faculty of the University of Zurich. A three-month digital coaching intervention was delivered via the smartphone application PEACH (Stieger et al., 2018 (Stieger et al., , 2021)), a chatbot-based digital coach that guides and supports users in pursuing personality change goals. Interested individuals downloaded the PEACH mobile application on their own smartphones. Eligibility required passing a screening and motivation to participate in the three-month digital personality change intervention (see Stieger et al., 2018, for details).

Eligible participants completed a pretest assessment and selected a personality change goal, supported by descriptions of typical characteristics associated with high and low trait levels.

In the intervention group, the pretest was followed by one week of experience sampling (ESM), 10 weeks of intervention, another week of ESM, and the posttest. In the waitlist control group, participants completed the pretest, waited four weeks, and then filled out the posttestfoot_0.

During the intervention, participants interacted with the chatbot daily, which delivered the interventional components. The intervention was grounded in the common change factors model (Allemand & Flückiger, 2017 , 2022), which highlights four key mechanisms for facilitating change: (a) increasing discrepancy awareness between current and desired traits, (b) activating personal strengths and resources and positive expectations, (c) fostering reflective processes to enhance insight, and (d) supporting behavioral practice to master new skills. The main goal of the change factor perspective is to optimally realize and integrate all four change factors to maximize intervention effects (Allemand & Flückiger, 2017 , 2022).

Weekly themes (e.g., building a support network, observational learning, identifying strengths) and microinterventions (e.g., implementation intentions, behavioral activation, self-reflection, individualized feedback) were designed to target these mechanisms.

Microinterventions combined shared techniques, such as reflection on behavioral successes and failures, with trait-specific strategies, for example, practicing extraverted behaviors when targeting Extraversion change (see Stieger et al., 2018 Stieger et al., , 2021 for more details). The exact content of the intervention therefore depended on participants' change goals.

Analytical Strategy

We used the EffectLiteR approach (Mayer et al., 2016 (Mayer et al., , 2020) ) to estimate the individual and average treatment effects. This approach is based on the specification and estimation of a multi-group structural equation model (MG-SEM) with selected baseline covariates and stochastic group sizes. Using this model, the expected value on the outcome variable in the intervention condition and the waitlist control condition is estimated for each person according to their values on the baseline covariates. The difference between these expected values is referred to as the conditional treatment effect (i.e., the treatment effect given a specific pattern of covariate values). Under certain assumptions, this effect can be interpreted as an individual treatment effect (see Mayer et al., 2020). The average treatment effect in the population, which is usually the focus, corresponds to the unconditional expectation of these conditional effects.

To implement the EffectLiteR approach, we followed several steps (see Supplemental Analytical Strategy for details): First, we specified multi-group measurement models for the outcome variables and the 26 multi-item covariates using full information maximum likelihood estimation. The different time intervals between measurements in the two groups (1 month in the waitlist control group and 3 months in the intervention group) were adjusted using a linear growth curve model. Second, based on factor scores and regression models predicting change in the outcome, we selected the covariates in two steps: The number of covariates (k) was determined using repeated 10-fold cross-validation with forward selection, benchmarked against a permutation-based null distribution. Which covariates filled these k positions was determined via complementary-pairs stability selection (Meinshausen & Bühlmann, 2010; Shah & Samworth, 2013), that is, by re-running the forward selection on random half-samples and retaining the k covariates selected most frequently. The selection targeted treatment × covariate interactions (i.e., potential moderators) while always retaining the baseline outcome, treatment, their interaction, and all covariate main effects in the regression models. Third, we estimated the final MG-SEMs with the selected covariates (Z) and used the intercept g0(Z) and effect g1(Z) functions to test for average treatment effects (null hypothesis: E[g1(Z)] = 0) and their heterogeneity across individuals (null hypothesis: g1(Z) = constant). Fourth, we calculated and visualized the individual treatment effects and estimated their bivariate relationships with all 34 baseline variables, with standard errors derived from a nonparametric bootstrap. The selected covariates thus provide the basis on which individual effects are modeled, whereas the subsequent characterization of who benefits draws on all baseline variables. Fifth, we probed the robustness of these analytic choices in four additional analyses: (a) backward instead of forward selection, (b) a covariate set defined by an error-controlling stability-selection threshold rather than by k, (c) a different assumption about the unobserved change process in the waitlist group (extrapolating the observed 1-month change assuming decelerating rather than linear growth), and (d) excluding potentially careless responders (based on even-odd consistency and longstring for BFI-2 SR and BFI-2-S OR, respectively) and winsorizing outliers (|z| > 3). Finally, in post hoc exploratory analyses, we re-estimated all models separately for each of the nine life domains (modeled as manifest single-item outcomes) and for a unified personality-change outcome (see Supplemental Analytical Strategy).

Transparency and Openness

We embrace the values of openness and transparency in science. We, therefore, report how we determined our sample size, all data exclusions (if any), all manipulations, and all measures used in the present analyses. The supplemental materials as well as the data and analysis code necessary to reproduce the reported results are available at https://osf.io/xmvhr.

The design of the study was preregistered (Stieger et al., 2018). The analyses were not preregistered due to their exploratory nature.

Results

Descriptive statistics and reliability estimates for all continuous baseline and outcome measures are reported in Supplemental Table S1.

Life Satisfaction

The cross-validated optimum contained no treatment × covariate interactions (k = 0), and the prediction error never fell below the permutation-based null band (Supplemental Figure S3). The final model therefore included only treatment and the baseline outcome (model fit: χ²(5) = 4.5, CFI = 1.00, RMSEA = .00, SRMR = .011). The average treatment effect on life satisfaction was positive but not significant (Estimate = 0.133, SE = 0.106, d = 0.121, p = .212), and there was no evidence for heterogeneity of individual treatment effects, Wald χ²(1) = 0.21, p = .648. The robustness analyses largely confirmed the null findings, with the only exception being that, under a decelerating rather than linear waitlist extrapolation, the average effect reached significance (p = .045).

Average Domain Satisfaction

The cross-validated optimum was k = 5 (Supplemental Figure S2), and the prediction error at k = 5 fell below the permutation-based null band, indicating better-than-chance prediction. The five covariates entering the final model were Sociability, Compassion, Intellectual Curiosity, Aesthetic Sensitivity, and Creative Imagination (see Supplemental Table S6 for the effect function). Sociability, Compassion, and Intellectual Curiosity exceeded the per-comparison stability threshold, and Sociability also exceeded the familywise threshold (Supplemental Table S3; see Supplemental Figure S5 for the selectionprobability paths). The final model fit the data well, χ²(130) = 228.7, CFI = .976, RMSEA = .042, SRMR = .041. The average treatment effect was positive and significant (Estimate = 0.158, SE = 0.075, d = 0.196, p = .035), and individual treatment effects differed significantly between participants, Wald χ²(6) = 19.34, p = .004. For 26.6% of participants, the model implied significantly positive individual effects, for 66.4% no significant effects, and for 7.0% negative effects (Figure 2). Individual Treatment Effects of PEACH Across Participants Note. Individual treatment effects of the PEACH intervention are plotted for each participant (Participant ID) and sorted from the most positive (left) to the most negative (right) effect. Significantly positive effects are shown in blue, significantly negative effects in red, and nonsignificant differences in gray. Error bars represent 95% confidence intervals. The horizontal line at 0 indicates no treatment effect.

The selected covariate set was highly robust to the selection algorithm and the waitlist extrapolation: backward selection recovered the identical five covariates, the threshold-based set comprised similar variables, and the different extrapolation across time reproduced the same five covariates. Further, the average effect and its heterogeneity remained significant in all three models (Supplemental Table S2). On the outlier-and carelessness-corrected data, the cross-validated optimum dropped to k = 0, yielding a baseline-only model with a significant average effect (Estimate = 0.151, SE = 0.074, p = .042) but no significant heterogeneity, Wald χ²(1) = 0.89, p = .347. To examine whether similar covariates would in principle be recovered in the corrected data, we conducted a post hoc re-estimation of this model with k fixed at 5 from the main model (which had a very similar MSE to k = 0). This yielded the identical five covariates, and both the average effect (Estimate = 0.147, SE = 0.072, p = .041) and the heterogeneity of individual effects (Wald χ²(6) = 19.84, p = .003) remained significant.

Across all baseline variables (Table 1), larger individual treatment effects on average domain satisfaction were associated with higher observer-reported Openness (r = .46, p = .011), male gender (r = -.21, p = .027), and lower baseline change goal attainability (r = -.25, p = .042). The association with self-reported Intellectual Curiosity was of similar size as observer-reported Openness but not significant (r = .49, p = .058). These associations were largely consistent across the robustness models. Observer-reported Openness was significant in five of six models, and gender and change goal attainability in four of six (Table 1). We decomposed each of the three robust correlates into model-implied expected outcomes (Supplemental Table S5). First, for gender, the average treatment effect was significant for men (0.249, p = .007) but not for women (0.080, p = .311; difference: -0.17, p = .027). Under the intervention, both women (0.173) and men (0.184) were expected to improve to a comparable degree, whereas under the control condition the expected change was more favorable for women (0.092) than for men (-0.064). Second, for observer-reported Openness, the positive association with individual treatment effects reflected both greater expected improvement under the intervention (r = .29, p = .014) and less expected improvement under the control condition (r = -.39, p = .003), with the same pattern for selfreported Intellectual Curiosity (intervention r = .37, p = .015; control r = -.40, p = .033).

Third, for change goal attainability, the negative association arose because higher attainability predicted greater expected improvement under the control condition (r = .25, p = .005) but was unrelated to expected change under the intervention (r = -.06, p = .551).

Note that the three robust correlates were not among the five covariates of the final model. Because the individual effects are a linear function of these covariates (Supplemental Table S6), the robust correlates are associated with individual effects only through their correlations with the covariates (r up to .74; see intercorrelation matrix at https://osf.io/xmvhr). They thus summarize the same pattern in terms of observable characteristics. The five covariates themselves showed some of the largest correlations in Table 1 (|r| = .34-.49, except Creative Imagination) but did not reach significance (p = .058-.124). In addition, their intercorrelations (r = .39-.65 among the Openness facets) render the individual coefficients of the effect function imprecise, which is why we characterize the heterogeneity through the bivariate associations rather than through these coefficients.

Finally, individual treatment effects were unrelated to participants' change goals, suggesting that differences in intervention content are unlikely to account for the observed heterogeneity.

Post Hoc Exploratory Analyses

At the domain level (Supplemental Table S4), individual treatment effects differed significantly between participants in eight of the nine domains (all ps ≤ .038) and marginally for sexual relationships (p = .052). Average treatment effects were significant only for the domains school/work (Estimate = 0.393, SE = 0.172, d = 0.159, p = .022) and daily emotions (Estimate = 0.479, SE = 0.174, d = 0.180, p = .006). For the unified personality-change outcome (Supplemental Table S4), the average treatment effect was relatively strong and significant (Estimate = 0.494, SE = 0.134, d = 0.267, p < .001), with no evidence for heterogeneity, Wald χ²(1) = 1.67, p = .196.

Discussion

In this study, we examined whether a 10-week digital personality change intervention, previously shown to lead to changes in personality traits (Stieger et al., 2021), causally influences life satisfaction, average domain satisfaction, and satisfaction with individual domains on average or for individuals with specific characteristics. Using the EffectLiteR framework (Mayer et al., 2016 (Mayer et al., , 2020)), we quantified both average and individual treatment effects. We then linked interindividual differences in treatment effects to baseline variables, including demographic characteristics, baseline personality traits, baseline well-being, motivational factors, and engagement preferences. This is consistent with exploring the prescriptive predictive value of baseline variables (Fournier et al., 2009). For life satisfaction, we found no evidence for an average effect or for heterogeneity of effects across individuals. However, for average domain satisfaction, the intervention yielded a positive average effect, concentrated in work-and emotion-related domains, accompanied by meaningful heterogeneity across participants, which was associated with interindividual differences assessed at baseline. In the following, we discuss these effects in light of previous research and outline implications, limitations, and fruitful avenues for future research.

Average Intervention Effects on Well-Being

The treatment effects were d = 0.12 for life satisfaction (not significant) and d = 0.20 for average domain satisfaction. The stronger treatment effects observed for average domain satisfaction, compared with life satisfaction, suggest that domain-based measures may be closer to the outcomes targeted by the intervention than the global judgment. Importantly, the two domains with significant average effects (satisfaction with school/work: d = 0.16; satisfaction with daily emotions: d = 0.18) are precisely those most plausibly tied to the change goals chosen by most participants (Increasing Conscientiousness, n = 226, and Decreasing Neuroticism, n = 256; together 55% of the sample).

The effects on satisfaction outcomes were somewhat smaller than the effect on personality traits (d = 0.27), consistent with satisfaction being a more distal outcome. They were also somewhat smaller than previously reported mean-level changes in satisfaction across the PEACH intervention period (Olaru, van Scheppingen, Stieger, et al., 2023; e.g., life satisfaction: d = 0.28, 0.23, and 0.21 for the change goal of Decreasing Neuroticism, Increasing Extraversion, and Increasing Conscientiousness, respectively). In contrast to these previous findings, we implemented a clear causal inference strategy by (a) using a novel method to estimate treatment effects (EffectLiteR) rather than pre-post mean-level changes, (b) adjusting for unequal pre-post intervals (3-month intervention vs. 1-month control), and (c) conducting (modified) intention-to-treat analyses, as is best practice for randomized controlled trials. Further, we included participants with all change goals, yielding a larger and more heterogeneous sample (N = 873 instead of N = 647). Using this approach, we find evidence that the intervention causally improves domain satisfaction, both on average and for individual domains, with slightly more conservative effect size estimates.

On a broader level, the causal relationships between volitional personality change and domain satisfaction established here carry two key implications: First, given that the traits targeted by the majority of participants (Decreasing Neuroticism, Increasing Extraversion, and Increasing Conscientiousness) are all robustly associated with higher domain-specific satisfaction across multiple life domains (Hudson & Roberts, 2014; Olaru, van Scheppingen, Bleidorn, et al., 2023), our results provide experimental confirmation of these wellestablished cross-sectional associations. This finding is in line with theories that assume causal effects of personality on well-being (e.g., Kroencke et al., 2023). Second, previous research has shown that dissatisfied individuals tend to report stronger change goals (Hudson & Roberts, 2014). Our findings suggest that for individuals with such change goals (an inclusion criterion for the intervention), personality change interventions may represent a promising, albeit modest, route to improving well-being.

Interindividual Differences in Intervention Effects

For life satisfaction, we did not find significant heterogeneity, whereas for average domain satisfaction, and for satisfaction with almost every individual domain, we did. The presence of heterogeneity is consistent with recent work in clinical psychology, which emphasizes that treatment effects can vary substantially across individuals (e.g., Cohen & DeRubeis, 2018; Kaiser et al., 2022). The fact that heterogeneity emerged for domain satisfaction but not life satisfaction reinforces previous arguments that domain-based measures may be more proximal to the intervention outcomes. The absence of heterogeneity in personality traits may indicate that the intervention changes personality relatively uniformly. However, it may also reflect methodological limitations (i.e., we combined the traits into a unified outcome variable because we lacked the power to analyze each change goal condition separately). Disentangling these accounts will require future studies sufficiently powered for trait-specific subgroup analyses (see Strengths, Limitations, and Future Outlook).

On a broader level, our results suggest that the significantly positive effects for average domain satisfaction described above only apply to 27% of participants, while 66% were expected to experience no significant effects and 7% even significantly negative effects. This finding critically extends recent research highlighting possible negative side effects of personality change interventions (Haehner et al., 2026), such as exhaustion from sustained counterdispositional behavior (Jacques-Hamilton et al., 2019), frustration over unmet goals, or increased self-doubt.

Interindividual Differences Moderating Intervention Effects

Given the accumulating evidence for intervention outcome heterogeneity, identifying prescriptive variables that indicate who might experience adverse effects is an essential next step to improve effectiveness, prevent potential harmful side effects, and disseminate interventions more responsibly. Among a broad set of interindividual differences, we identified three prescriptive variables that were robustly associated with stronger well-being increases in the treatment compared to the control condition and that summarize, in terms of directly observable characteristics, the heterogeneity captured by the personality facets in the final model. As our analysis approach was exploratory, the results should be considered a promising starting point for future confirmatory research, and we can only provide tentative explanations for the observed effects.

First, treatment effects were positive and significant for men, but small and nonsignificant for women. A closer examination showed that this difference was driven almost entirely by the control condition rather than by differential responses to the intervention itself. Women, but not men, tended to improve even without the intervention, possibly by seeking psychological support elsewhere, consistent with evidence that men culturally engage in less help-seeking (Addis & Mahalik, 2003).

Second, participants with higher Openness benefited more from the intervention, consistent with some previous findings from positive psychology interventions (Senf & Liau, 2013). This association was most robust for observer-reported Openness and pointed in the same direction for the self-reported facet Intellectual Curiosity. More open individuals improved more under the intervention, possibly because their curiosity and willingness to try new things led them to engage more deeply with the intervention content. At the same time, they improved less without the intervention, suggesting that their curiosity may require structured input to translate into change.

Third, change goal attainability was positively related to expected improvement under the control condition but unrelated to expected improvement under the intervention, indicating that participants who saw their goal as attainable tended to improve even without the intervention, whereas those who saw it as less attainable depended on it. For these individuals, the intervention may supply the goal-relevant resources that they otherwise lack in their everyday environments (e.g., situational opportunities to enact the goal, a sense of personal control, and reliable social support).

Regarding baseline well-being, we did not find the negative moderation effect suggested by prior clinical work. A plausible account is a non-linear (inverted-U) relation: Individuals with intermediate baseline well-being benefit most, whereas those with high baseline well-being show ceiling effects and those with very low baseline well-being require more intensive interventions (e.g., psychotherapy; Gander et al., 2016). Similarly, other motivational factors (e.g., implicit theory of personality) and engagement preferences did not robustly predict treatment effects. This parallels findings from the same intervention that change goal strength, attainability, and beliefs about the changeability of personality did not consistently predict personality change during the intervention (Olaru et al., 2025). Overall, despite observing significant outcome heterogeneity and examining a broad set of interindividual difference variables at baseline, we found few significant associations.

Moreover, although the heterogeneity itself could be demonstrated with high confidence, identifying the covariates responsible for it was subject to larger uncertainty. This pattern is in line with previous research showing that heterogeneity in treatment effects is difficult to predict (Kaiser et al., 2022; von Hippel & Schuetze, 2025) and points to a need for further work in this area (see Strengths, Limitations, and Future Outlook).

Implications

In our study, we used a causal inference framework to calculate individual treatment effects of the intervention vs. control group, instead of simply predicting observed pre-post differences in the intervention group. Our findings illustrate why this matters: Expected improvement under the intervention was nearly identical for women and men and unrelated to change goal attainability, so a prognostic analysis within the intervention group would have missed both associations, which arose from differences in improvement without the intervention. Thus, the results on prescriptive variables are particularly informative for personalizing intervention choice. First, our results suggest that personality change interventions offer the greatest added value for men, individuals who are rated higher in Openness by others, and those who perceive their change goal as less attainable. For women and for individuals with below-average observer-reported Openness, expected treatment effects were essentially null (see Supplemental Table S5). For women, however, this does not mean that the intervention is ineffective in absolute terms, as they improved under the intervention as much as men did but also improved without it. Only at very low Openness levels may effects be negative (cf. the 7% of participants with significantly negative individual effects), suggesting that interventions should be administered more cautiously in this group. Second, researchers could work on developing alternative interventions for individuals who might experience null or even negative effects by either adjusting existing interventions or by suggesting entirely different intervention strategies (e.g., acceptance-or strength-based approaches; Krämer et al., 2025; Peterson & Seligman, 2004). As noted above, however, both implications ultimately depend on replicating these exploratory findings in confirmatory research (see also Meinke et al., 2024).

Strengths, Limitations, and Future Outlook

Our study has several strengths. This work represents the first investigation of heterogeneous treatment effects of personality change interventions on well-being.

Importantly, we examined the prescriptive value of baseline variables, which can specifically inform personalized intervention choice but is rarely examined. Moreover, we used data from the largest randomized controlled personality intervention to date (Stieger et al., 2018 (Stieger et al., , 2021)), providing an exceptionally high-powered analysis. Our analysis strategy is also consistent with recent methodological recommendations to separate true heterogeneity from estimation noise, benchmark against explicit null distributions, and treat significance claims from many candidate moderators with caution (von Hippel & Schuetze, 2025). Naturally, however, this work is subject to several limitations, which point to interesting directions for future research.

First, given that this is a secondary data analysis, we encountered several challenges inherent to the original study design. For instance, the time lag of outcome measurements differed between the intervention group (3 months) and control group (1 month), which we accounted for using a linear growth curve model. This choice mildly affected the results. For life satisfaction, for instance, the average effect became significant under the alternative extrapolation. Future studies should preregister such analytic decisions and the entire data analysis pipeline in advance.

Second, attrition was substantial (39%), as is common in digital interventions.

Because all 873 participants entered the analyses via full information maximum likelihood and dropout was only weakly related to observed baseline traits (Stieger et al., 2021), we consider the risk of bias limited. However, bias from unobserved determinants of dropout cannot be ruled out, and the effects may generalize primarily to settings with comparable adherence.

Third, while we explicitly opted for an exploratory analysis approach to accommodate our goal of simultaneously evaluating a wide range of potential interindividual difference moderators, our results require confirmation in an independent sample and ideally with a hypothesis-confirming approach. Given the scarcity of randomized controlled personality intervention studies conducted to date, this will require substantial further research with samples large enough to accommodate moderation analyses. Because covariates were selected on the same data, the reported p values of correlates (Table 1) are conditional on that selection and thus exploratory. We therefore gauge each association by its consistency across models rather than in isolation. Fifth, while we examined a broad range of baseline variables spanning sociodemographic, personality, and motivational factors, our selection of variables was naturally limited by the available data. Other potentially important variables are promising targets for future investigations. In particular, future work should study the role of ethnicity and culture-related variables to ensure that personality change interventions benefit diverse populations. Importantly, the estimate of heterogeneity depends on the diversity of the sample and is only accurate if all relevant covariates were included. Accordingly, studies using larger, more heterogeneous samples and a broader set of baseline variables may uncover even greater interindividual differences.

Conclusion

This study provides the first investigation of interindividual differences in well-being effects of digital personality change interventions. While the investigated intervention improved average domain satisfaction for a typical individual, particularly in work-and emotion-related domains, we identified remarkable heterogeneity in individual treatment effects on well-being. Among a broad range of potential correlates, gender, observer-reported Openness, and self-reported change goal attainability were associated with these effects. These findings underscore that personality change interventions cannot be assumed to work equally well for all individuals. Future research should investigate more diverse populations, identify further important moderator variables, and, crucially, develop personalization strategies that maximize benefits, minimize harm, and ensure inclusivity.

Figure1 ;1 = very dissatisfied to5 = very satisfied): (a) school/work, (b) financial situation, (c) family relationship, (d) health, (e) sexual relationships, (f) recreational activities, (g) friendships, (h) emotions experienced on a daily basis, and (i) oneself as a person.

To obtain our focal outcome measure (i.e., average domain satisfaction), we modeled the average of all domainspecific satisfactions (see Analytical Strategy). This is consistent with bottom-up theories of well-being, which conceptualize life satisfaction as a summary of domain-specific experiences (see Introduction). Moreover, it reduces alpha error inflation by minimizing the number of statistical tests, attenuates single-item measurement error, and enables latentvariable modeling within the EffectLiteR framework. The BFI-2 self-report was also administered at posttest and served as the basis for the unified personality-change outcome (see Analytical Strategy).

Fourth

Future research should recruit even larger and especially more heterogeneous samples to (a) evaluate whether the findings generalize to other age groups (e.g., adolescents) and different cultural contexts, and (b) enable analyses that require even more data points, including comparisons between different intervention groups (e.g., change goals of Decreasing Neuroticism vs. Increasing Extraversion) or tests of curvilinear associations with individual treatment effects.
